fetched_contents.text: Food selectivity and autism: A systematic review Abstract BACKGROUND Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder that manifests in the first years of life, with a complex pathogenesis influenced by biological, genetic and epigenetic factors. Many children with ASD display marked food selectivity, often restricting themselves to a narrow range of foods. The problems associated with feeding children with ASD can vary widely, from mild cases that pose no immediate health risks, to more severe situations with a risk of malnutrition or, conversely, overeating. This scoping review aims to provide an in-depth overview of the frequency, nature and factors related to food selectivity in children with autism. AIM To comprehensively review the literature on food selectivity in ASD. METHODS A systematic review of the literature was conducted using the PubMed, Web of Science and EBSCO databases, to identify articles published in English from 2014 until 2024. Studies on a sample diagnosed with ASD and food selectivity were included. The selected databases were chosen for their broad coverage of the scientific literature. These databases represent reliable sources of high-quality articles, ensuring a comprehensive and up-to-date search. RESULTS We evaluated 222 studies on food selectivity in autism, from which duplicates were removed and unrelated titles were filtered out. Finally, 9 articles were included in the review. Five articles provide a general overview of the phenomenon, analysing its nature and factors. Two studies delve into sensory sensitivity, in particular the impact of food textures, tastes and smells. Finally, two studies focus on problem behaviour during mealtimes. CONCLUSION Children with ASD have greater food selectivity than the neurotypical population. The diet should contain a greater variety of fruit, vegetables, yoghurt, while reducing the consumption of rice and pasta. Keywords: Food selectivity, Autism, Development, Autism spectrum disorder, Children ---------------------------------------- Core Tip: This scoping review explored food selectivity in autism spectrum disorder. Two main themes emerged: Eating behaviour (e.g., food refusal) during meals and sensory processing, in particular the smell, texture, taste, colour and temperature of food. Children with autism spectrum disorder have greater food selectivity than children with typical development and this makes them nutritionally vulnerable. INTRODUCTION Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neuro-developmental disorder with onset in early childhood with a complex pathogenesis, linked to biological, genetic and epigenetic factors[1,2]. The term ‘spectrum’ refers to the heterogeneity in the clinical manifestation and severity of ASD symptoms[3]. It is a condition characterised by difficulties in social interactions, both verbal and non-verbal communication, stereotyped behaviour and narrow interests[4]. The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th edition (DSM-5), groups the first two elements into a single social and communicative domain and narrow interests and repetitive behaviour[5]. In the child’s first year of life, a number of alarm bells can already be observed in order to identify typical or atypical development, such as, for example, a sociable smile or avoidance of a direct gaze. ASD can also be classified into three levels of severity: Level 1 (mild autism), level 2 (requires substantial support) and level 3 (the most severe form of autism)[6]. In the early understanding of autism, specific difficulties in executive functions are also present. In reality, the executive functions in autism are diverse and show individual variations, but no impairment or impairment is present compared to individuals with typical development[7]. International epidemiological studies have reported a widespread increase in the prevalence of ASD[8]. Approximately 1 in 100 children worldwide has an ASD[9]. Furthermore, although estimates indicate that men are more frequently diagnosed with autism than women, recent evidence suggests a tendency for under-diagnosis of autism in women[10], who have a more internalised autism syndrome, rather than a lower prevalence than men[11]. Many children with an ASD may display a strong selectivity towards food, often limiting themselves to an extremely small number of accepted foods, sometimes as few as five or less. Feeding difficulties are commonly reported in early childhood when, during mealtimes, young children venture to explore food through their senses, gradually acquiring greater self-awareness through the sensory experiences of taste, touch and smell[12]. However, inappropriate feeding practices may entail risks, including a slowdown in the child’s growth[13,14]. Problems related to food intake in children can manifest themselves in a wide range of facets, ranging from mild cases where the behaviour does not pose an immediate health risk, to more serious situations where there is a serious risk of malnutrition or, conversely, of exceeding the recommended intake[15]. In the DSM-5, nutrition and eating disorders are grouped into a single diagnostic category and are characterised by a persistent eating disorder or eating-related behaviour that results in impaired food consumption or intake and significantly impairs physical health or psychosocial functioning[3]. This means that, instead of promoting a balance in the diet, restrictions may feed an overwhelming desire for foods considered ‘forbidden’[2]. fetched_contents.text: A Scoping Review of Tools to Assess Diet in Children and Adolescents with Autism Spectrum Disorder Abstract Eating is considered one of the activities of daily living most affected by autism spectrum disorder (ASD) in children and adolescents and, therefore, needs to be thoroughly assessed using specific tools. The aim of this scoping review was to describe the most widely used tool to assess diet in children and adolescents with ASD. A search was conducted on PubMed, Scopus, EMBASE, Web of Science and PsycINFO databases. Two authors screened the articles and included all randomized or non-randomized studies published in English or Spanish in the last five years in which the diet of children and adolescents with ASD was assessed. Fifteen studies were included in this review. Mealtime behaviour was the most assessed variable in the included studies (n = 7). Thirteen different assessment tools were identified to evaluate the diet of children and adolescents with ASD, mainly at ages 2–12 (n = 11). The Brief Assessment scale for Mealtime Behavior in Children (BAMBI) and 24-h recalls were the most commonly used dietary assessment tools in the included studies. Our results can help professionals in the selection of an optimal scale to assess diet in children and adolescents with ASD. Keywords: neurodevelopmental disorders, childhood, questionnaires, diet, evaluation 1. Introduction Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is defined as a neurodevelopmental disorder mainly characterized by persistent deficits in social communication, difficulties in social interaction and a predisposition towards a pattern of stereotyped behaviours, interests and activities [1]. The etiological factors are diverse, and include epigenetic and environmental agents, although the definitive cause of ASD remains unknown [2,3]. These disorders manifest themselves at an early age, but are usually diagnosed later in childhood, at approximately 4 years of age [4]. According to the 2023 Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) report, the United States prevalence of ASD is 1 in 36 children, it is higher in boys than in girls and is continuously increasing [5,6]. Eating is one of the most affected daily life activities among children and adolescents with ASD, mainly because they tend to present hypersensitivity to some food textures, colours or tastes, which prevent them from trying new and unfamiliar foods [7,8]. This sensory alteration is usually manifested as repetitive, problematic and challenging behaviours at mealtimes, which may result in a restricted diet in terms of number and variety of foods [9,10,11]. This unvaried diet can even lead to nutrient inadequacy [12,13] and overweight [14,15], both of which can have negative effects on children’s and adolescents’ health [16]. Thus, there is an urgent need to develop dietary assessment tools for children and adolescents with ASD, which can be completed by parents and caregivers, to achieve a more accurate intervention in this issue. There is evidence which supports that existing standardised methods for assessing feeding problems, eating behaviours and diet quality in ASD are very limited [17,18]. As dietary patterns are established in childhood and continue into adulthood [19], it is important to know and to use valid assessment tools to evaluate diet at an early age to identify the main nutrition necessities and to promote an optimal intervention. Currently, there are some published reviews on dietary assessment tools in children and adolescents with ASD. De Souza Silva et al. [20] carried out a Systematic Review (SR) aimed at evaluating the methodological quality of dietary assessment methods used to evaluate the diet intake of children and adolescents with ASD in clinical and epidemiological studies. This SR included eighty-nine articles and the results showed that most of them had a low-quality score. Holloway et al. [21] carried out a Scoping Review aimed at examining the evidence of validity and availability of measurement tools that evaluate usual dietary intakes and physical activity behaviours among individuals with ASD. In this review, one hundred and thirteen articles were included, and the results showed the need for more validated dietary tools in the ASD population. In this sense, we seek to perform a Scoping Review to complement the existent scientific evidence by answering the following research question: Which tool has been the most used to assess the diet of children and adolescents with ASD in intervention studies published in the last five years? The objective of this Scoping Review is to provide physicians and researchers with an updated source of information on the most widely used dietary assessment tool for children and adolescents with ASD. 2. We conducted this type of review because our research question is broad and therefore could not have been addressed by a Systematic Review (SR). SRs are used to answer specific research questions which are usually related to the effectiveness, costs or effects of particular interventions [24,25]. Published in final edited form as: J Am Diet Assoc. 2010 Feb;110(2):238–246. doi: 10.1016/j.jada.2009.10.032 Abstract Autism spectrum disorders (ASDs) comprise a complex set of related developmental disorders that are characterized by impairments in communication, social interaction, and repetitive behaviors. Impairments in sensory processing are also extremely common. The prevalence of ASDs is increasing and is currently estimated to affect 1 in 150 children. ASDs are considered to be a major health and educational problem, affecting many areas of daily living, including eating. Children with ASDs are often described as picky or selective eaters. This paper provides a comprehensive narrative review of the empirical literature over the last 25 years on food selectivity and nutritional adequacy in children with ASDs. The possible contributions of sensory factors, such as sensory sensitivity, to food selectivity are discussed. The need for an interdisciplinary approach to managing atypical eating patterns in children with ASD is highlighted. Keywords: autism, food selectivity, sensory sensitivity INTRODUCTION Early childhood is a period when children experience new foods, tastes, and textures. Parents of toddlers and young children often describe their children as “picky eaters”, refusing to try or eat a variety of foods. Although picky eating is not uncommon among young children who are typically developing, pickiness in children with autism spectrum disorders (ASDs) may be even more restrictive and may extend beyond the early childhood period (1–3). Research on feeding behaviors in children with autism uses a mix of objective and subjective documentation methods, with a strong emphasis on parent-reported and observational tools that capture mealtime behavior, food refusal, and dietary intake.

Common assessment tools include the Brief Assessment scale for Mealtime Behavior in Children (BAMBI) and 24-h recalls, which are among the most commonly used dietary assessment tools in ASD studies [N2-F2]. Another example is an instrument that assesses nutritional aspects across seven domains, including feeding behavior, dietary intake, daily routines, and clinical aspects [N2-R2]. A scoping review of diet assessment tools in children and adolescents with ASD identified 13 different assessment tools, mainly targeting ages 2–12, with BAMBI and 24-h recalls appearing most frequently [N2-F2]. The tools are typically used in studies published in English or Spanish and often rely on standardized methods for scoring, though the evidence here does not provide detailed scoring algorithms for all tools [N2-F2].

Objective documentation is limited in the evidence provided, but some studies use food records, questionnaires, interviews, or actual food intake observations to assess dietary intake and mealtime behavior [N3-F3]. One study observed actual food intake, manipulating food type, while most studies depend on parent report or other self-reported measures [N3-F3]. This suggests a reliance on subjective documentation in many cases, with objective methods used sparingly. The evidence also notes that existing standardized methods for assessing feeding problems and eating behaviors in ASD are very limited, and that dietary assessment tools are often completed by parents and caregivers to improve intervention accuracy [N2-F2].

Nutrient intake and eating frequency are linked to behavior through the documentation of mealtime behavior and dietary intake. The scoping review emphasizes that mealtime behavior is the most assessed variable in included studies, and that sensory alterations can lead to restricted diet, nutrient inadequacy, overweight, and other negative health effects [N2-F2]. Similarly, the narrative review states that food selectivity may be associated with inadequate nutrition because of restricted diet, and that restricted intake can lead to nutrient inadequacy [N3-F3]. The evidence therefore supports the idea that feeding behavior documentation is used to infer not only meal patterns but also nutritional consequences such as deficiencies, overweight, and poor growth [N2-F2][N3-F3].

Overall, the documentation approach is mixed: many studies use standardized assessment tools and parent-reported data, while objective measures are less common and more limited in scope [N2-F2][N3-F3]. Nutrient intake and eating frequency are documented through dietary assessment tools and observational/measurement methods, and behavioral data are used to explain variations in intake and health outcomes [N2-F2][N3-F3].

Repeatedly observed feeding behavior patterns in children with autism include mealtime resistance, food refusal, sensory and texture-related issues, and dietary restrictions and food preferences.

Mealtime resistance and refusal are central. A scoping review of diet assessment tools notes that mealtime behavior was the most assessed variable in the included studies [N2-F2]. Another review describes atypical eating behavior as food refusal, selectivity, or unusual mealtime behaviors and notes that children with ASD often refuse foods on the basis of their features [N3-F3][N3-R5]. A separate study found that children with ASD were more likely to refuse foods than typically developing controls [N3-R5]. These sources together indicate that mealtime resistance and refusal are common and widely documented in ASD research.

Sensory and texture-related feeding issues are also prevalent. The narrative review explicitly links food selectivity to sensory factors such as smell, texture, color, and temperature, and describes children with ASD as being highly selective eaters with very restricted repertoires of food acceptance [N3-F3]. It also states that sensory processing difficulties are extremely common in ASD and that these may extend beyond early childhood [N3-F3]. A separate source adds that mealtime behaviors can be affected by sensory processing challenges, with children resisting certain foods or resisting using utensils [N3-R4]. Taken together, the evidence supports that sensory sensitivity and texture aversion are major contributors to feeding difficulties in this population [N3-F3][N3-R4].

Dietary restrictions and food preferences are another recurring pattern. The same narrative review reports that children with ASD often have very restricted repertoires of food acceptance, sometimes limited to as few as five foods [N3-F3]. Another study notes that food selectivity may extend beyond early childhood and that picky eating may be associated with inadequate nutrition because of the restricted diet [N3-F3]. The scoping review also notes that restricted diet can lead to nutrient inadequacy and overweight [N2-F2]. These findings indicate that dietary restrictions and strong food preferences are common, and they are often tied to both behavioral and nutritional consequences [N3-F3][N2-F2].

Taken as a whole, the most consistently observed patterns are mealtime resistance/refusal, sensory and texture-related feeding issues, and dietary restrictions with highly restricted food preferences [N2-F2][N3-F3][N3-R5]. These patterns are repeated across multiple sources and are framed as central features of feeding difficulties in ASD [N3-R5][N3-F3].

Documentation also guides dietary and behavioral interventions. The evidence notes that treatment plans aim to balance essential nutrient intake while accounting for sensory sensitivities and food preferences [N4-R2]. Feeding therapy is explicitly linked to improving nutrition and building healthier eating habits [N4-R4]. The MEAL Plan provides specific strategies for managing eating aversions and expanding dietary diversity [N4-R3]. This indicates that documentation of feeding behavior is not merely descriptive but is intended to inform targeted dietary and behavioral interventions [N4-R2][N4-R4][N4-R3].

However, the evidence also points to limitations and gaps. The scoping review on diet assessment tools emphasizes that existing standardized methods for assessing feeding problems and eating behaviors in ASD are very limited [N2-F2]. The same review notes that dietary assessment tools are often completed by parents and caregivers, which may improve intervention accuracy but does not eliminate subjectivity or measurement limitations [N2-F2]. The narrative review further notes that food selectivity has not been operationally defined consistently and has been used to refer to picky eating, frequent food refusals, limited food variety, excessive intake of a few foods, and selective intake of certain food categories [N3-F3]. ## Integrated synthesis of how feeding behaviors are systematically categorized and documented in autism research

Research on feeding behaviors among children with autism is organized around a combination of systematic categorization, measurement documentation, observed patterns, clinical use, and nutritional outcomes. Across the evidence provided, feeding behaviors are not treated as a single phenomenon but as a multidimensional problem involving mealtime behavior, food selectivity, sensory processing, and dietary restriction. The documentation methods are also mixed, with strong reliance on parent-reported and observational tools, alongside limited objective measures. Overall, the field is shaped by both clinical practice and research: feeding behavior documentation is used to identify problems, guide intervention, and explain health and nutritional consequences, but it is also constrained by inconsistent definitions and measurement limitations.

### 1) Systematic categorization of feeding behaviors

Feeding behaviors in autism research are systematically categorized into several major domains. The most consistent dimensions are **mealtime behavior**, **food selectivity**, and **sensory processing**, with **restrictive or repetitive eating patterns** also recurring as a key category.

- **Mealtime behavior** is central to classification. A scoping review notes that mealtime behavior was the most assessed variable in included studies, and that sensory alterations can lead to restricted diet, nutrient inadequacy, overweight, and negative health effects [N2-F2]. Another review describes atypical eating behavior as food refusal, selectivity, or unusual mealtime behaviors [N3-F3]. This shows that mealtime behavior is treated as a broad behavioral domain rather than a single isolated issue [N2-F2][N3-F3].
- **Food selectivity** is another major dimension. The narrative review states that children with ASD often display marked food selectivity, often restricting themselves to a narrow range of foods [N3-F3]. It also defines food selectivity as picky eating, frequent food refusals, limited food variety, excessive intake of a few foods, and selective intake of certain food categories [N3-F3]. A systematic review similarly notes that children diagnosed with ASD have a higher incidence of feeding problems and food selectivity than the neurotypical population [N1-F1]. Thus, food selectivity is a core category used to classify feeding difficulties in ASD [N3-F3][N1-F1].
- **Sensory processing** is a recurring explanatory framework. The narrative review explicitly links food selectivity to sensory sensitivity, noting that smell, texture, color, and temperature can contribute to food selectivity [N3-F3]. It also emphasizes that sensory processing difficulties are extremely common in ASD [N3-F3]. A broader systematic review similarly highlights that children with ASD may display distinctive feeding difficulties and atypical feeding behaviors, including picky eating, limited independent feeding, and need for assistance [N1-R5]. So, sensory processing is often treated as a broader framework that helps explain feeding behavior rather than a separate category [N3-F3][N1-R5].
- **Restrictive or repetitive eating patterns** are also prominent. These patterns are often described through food refusal, limited food variety, and repetitive mealtime behaviors [N3-F3][N3-R5]. The evidence suggests that feeding behaviors in ASD are frequently organized around how children limit their eating repertoire and how that relates to mealtime resistance [N3-F3][N3-R5].

In studies versus broader frameworks, categories are sometimes operationalized differently. In studies, food selectivity is often measured through parent reports, food records, questionnaires, interviews, or actual food intake observation [N3-F3]. In broader frameworks, feeding behavior is categorized into mealtime behavior, food selectivity, and sensory processing, with the latter serving as an explanatory dimension rather than a standalone behavior [N2-F2][N3-F3]. The evidence also shows that definitions can be inconsistent across studies; for example, food selectivity is described as picky eating, frequent refusals, limited variety, and selective intake, rather than a single homogeneous construct [N3-F3].

Age and severity differences are implied in the evidence, though less directly. The scoping review notes that assessment tools were mainly used for children and adolescents aged 2–12 [N2-F2]. The narrative review suggests that food selectivity may extend beyond early childhood and that severity of feeding problems may vary, with some cases posing mild risks and others serious risks of malnutrition or overeating [N3-F1][N3-F3]. The systematic review on feeding problems in ASD reports that feeding problems were found in 61% of children with ASD and in 46.4% of children with ID, with children with ASD showing more disruptive mealtime behavior [N1-R3]. Taken together, the evidence suggests that feeding behavior categories are applied across age groups, but the literature often focuses on early childhood and adolescents, and severity differences are inferred from the range of outcomes, such as malnutrition versus overeating [N2-F2][N3-F3][N1-R3].

### 2) Documentation and measurement of feeding behaviors

Feeding behaviors are documented and measured using a mix of **objective** and **subjective** approaches, with **parent-reported and observational tools** playing a dominant role.

- **Common assessment tools** include the Brief Assessment scale for Mealtime Behavior in Children (BAMBI) and 24-h recalls, which are among the most commonly used dietary assessment tools in ASD studies [N2-F2]. Another example is an instrument that assesses nutritional aspects across seven domains, including feeding behavior, dietary intake, daily routines, and clinical aspects [N2-R2]. A scoping review of diet assessment tools in children and adolescents with ASD identified 13 different assessment tools, mainly targeting ages 2–12, with BAMBI and 24-h recalls appearing most frequently [N2-F2]. These tools are often used in studies published in English or Spanish and often rely on standardized methods for scoring, though the evidence here does not provide detailed scoring algorithms for all tools [N2-F2].
- **Objective documentation is limited**, but some studies use food records, questionnaires, interviews, or actual food intake observation to assess dietary intake and mealtime behavior [N3-F3]. One study observed actual food intake, manipulating food type, while most studies depend on parent report or other self-reported measures [N3-F3]. This suggests a reliance on subjective documentation in many cases, with objective methods used sparingly [N3-F3].

Nutrient intake and eating frequency are linked to behavior through the documentation of mealtime behavior and dietary intake. The scoping review emphasizes that mealtime behavior is the most assessed variable in included studies, and that sensory alterations can lead to restricted diet, nutrient inadequacy, overweight, and other negative health effects [N2-F2]. Similarly, the narrative review states that food selectivity may be associated with inadequate nutrition because of restricted diet, and that restricted intake can lead to nutrient inadequacy [N3-F3]. The evidence therefore supports the idea that feeding behavior documentation is used to infer not only meal patterns but also nutritional consequences such as deficiencies, overweight, and poor growth [N2-F2][N3-F3].

Overall, the documentation approach is mixed: many studies use standardized assessment tools and parent-reported data, while objective measures are less common and more limited in scope [N2-F2][N3-F3]. Nutrient intake and eating frequency are documented through dietary assessment tools and observational/measurement methods, and behavioral data are used to explain variations in intake and health outcomes [N2-F2][N3-F3].

### 3) Repeatedly observed feeding behavior patterns

Across the evidence, several feeding behavior patterns are repeatedly observed in children with autism:

- **Mealtime resistance or refusal** is central. A scoping review notes that mealtime behavior was the most assessed variable in included studies [N2-F2]. Another review describes atypical eating behavior as food refusal, selectivity, or unusual mealtime behaviors and notes that children with ASD often refuse foods on the basis of their features [N3-F3][N3-R5]. A separate study found that children with ASD were more likely to refuse foods than typically developing controls [N3-R5]. These sources together indicate that mealtime resistance and refusal are common and widely documented in ASD research [N2-F2][N3-F3][N3-R5].
- **Sensory and texture-related feeding issues** are also prevalent. The narrative review explicitly links food selectivity to sensory factors such as smell, texture, color, and temperature [N3-F3]. It also states that sensory processing difficulties are extremely common in ASD and that these may extend beyond early childhood [N3-F3]. A separate source adds that mealtime behaviors can be affected by sensory processing challenges, with children resisting certain foods or resisting using utensils [N3-R4]. Taken together, the evidence supports that sensory sensitivity and texture aversion are major contributors to feeding difficulties in this population [N3-F3][N3-R4].
- **Dietary restrictions and food preferences** are another recurring pattern. The same narrative review reports that children with ASD often have very restricted repertoires of food acceptance, sometimes limited to as few as five foods [N3-F3]. Another study notes that food selectivity may extend beyond early childhood and that picky eating may be associated with inadequate nutrition because of the restricted diet [N3-F3]. The scoping review also notes that restricted diet can lead to nutrient inadequacy and overweight [N2-F2]. These findings indicate that dietary restrictions and strong food preferences are common, and they are often tied to both behavioral and nutritional consequences [N3-F3][N2-F2].

In summary, the most consistently observed patterns are **mealtime resistance/refusal**, **sensory and texture-related feeding issues**, and **dietary restrictions with highly restricted food preferences** [N2-F2][N3-F3][N3-R5]. These patterns are repeated across multiple sources and are framed as central features of feeding difficulties in ASD [N3-R5][N3-F3].

### 4) How feeding behavior documentation informs clinical care and intervention

Feeding behavior documentation is used in treatment planning and intervention guidance. Nutrition and feeding therapy for children on the autism spectrum is described as ensuring children receive essential nutrients while considering sensory sensitivities and food preferences [N4-R2]. Similarly, feeding therapy is described as helping children improve nutrition, reduce mealtime stress, and build healthier eating habits [N4-R4]. The Autism MEAL Plan is an explicit example of a treatment-oriented intervention that includes education on feeding issues, behavior management, and strategies to expand dietary diversity [N4-R3]. These examples show that feeding behavior documentation is directly used to shape intervention strategies, particularly through dietary and behavioral approaches [N4-R2][N4-R4][N4-R3].

Documentation also guides **dietary and behavioral interventions**. The evidence notes that treatment plans aim to balance essential nutrient intake while accounting for sensory sensitivities and food preferences [N4-R2]. Feeding therapy is explicitly linked to improving nutrition and building healthier eating habits [N4-R4]. The MEAL Plan provides specific strategies for managing eating aversions and expanding dietary diversity [N4-R3]. This indicates that documentation of feeding behavior is not merely descriptive but is intended to inform targeted dietary and behavioral interventions [N4-R2][N4-R4][N4-R3].

However, the evidence also points to **limitations and gaps** in clinical documentation. The scoping review on diet assessment tools emphasizes that existing standardized methods for assessing feeding problems and eating behaviors in ASD are very limited [N2-F2]. The same review notes that dietary assessment tools are often completed by parents and caregivers, which may improve intervention accuracy but does not eliminate subjectivity or measurement limitations [N2-F2]. The narrative review further notes that food selectivity has not been operationally defined consistently and has been used to refer to picky eating, frequent food refusals, limited food variety, excessive intake of a few foods, and selective intake of certain food categories [N3-F3]. This inconsistency in definition and measurement suggests that documentation can be incomplete or imprecise, which limits its utility in clinical decision-making [N3-F3].

In short, feeding behavior documentation informs treatment planning and intervention by guiding dietary and behavioral strategies, but the evidence indicates that standardized, objective documentation is limited and that definitions and measurement approaches are inconsistent [N2-F2][N4-R2][N4-R4][N4-R3][N3-F3].

### 5) Dietary and nutrient outcomes associated with feeding behavior patterns

The evidence indicates that feeding behavior patterns are closely linked to **nutrient inadequacy**, **overweight**, and **growth-related effects**.

- **Common nutrient deficiencies or intake patterns linked to feeding behaviors** include nutrient inadequacy and restricted intake. The narrative review states that food selectivity may be associated with inadequate nutrition because of restricted diet, and that restricted intake can lead to nutrient inadequacy [N3-F3]. The scoping review on diet assessment tools similarly notes that restricted diet can lead to nutrient inadequacy and overweight [N2-F2]. Another study notes that children with ASD and severe food selectivity may be at increased risk for nutritional inadequacies [N6-R2]. These findings support the idea that feeding behavior patterns are closely tied to inadequate nutrient intake [N3-F3][N2-F2][N6-R2].
- **Behavioral documentation is used to predict or explain growth and health outcomes**. The scoping review links mealtime behavior to nutrient inadequacy, overweight, and negative health effects [N2-F2]. The narrative review similarly links sensory sensitivity and food selectivity to inadequate nutrition and to the potential for restricted diet to lead to nutrient inadequacy and overweight [N3-F3]. The evidence also notes that persistent avoidance or refusal can contribute to poor growth [N1-F1]. Taken together, the documentation of feeding behavior is used to explain not only immediate meal patterns but also broader health outcomes such as nutrient status, weight, and growth [N2-F2][N3-F3][N1-F1].
- **Differences in documentation quality across studies and settings** are evident. The scoping review emphasizes that existing standardized methods for assessing feeding problems and eating behaviors in ASD are very limited [N2-F2]. It also notes that dietary assessment tools are often completed by parents and caregivers, which may improve intervention accuracy but does not eliminate subjectivity or measurement limitations [N2-F2]. The narrative review states that food selectivity has not been operationally defined consistently, and that it has been used to refer to multiple related phenomena, including picky eating, frequent refusals, limited variety, and selective intake [N3-F3]. These inconsistencies suggest that documentation quality varies by study design, measurement approach, and the setting in which the data are collected [N2-F2][N3-F3].

### 6) Integrated conclusion

In autism research, feeding behaviors are systematically categorized around **mealtime behavior**, **food selectivity**, **sensory processing**, and **restrictive eating patterns**. These categories are often used interchangeably in studies, but they also differ in how they are defined and measured. The documentation approach is mixed: many studies rely on **parent-reported and observational tools**, while objective measures are less common and more limited in scope [N2-F2][N3-F3]. The most repeatedly observed patterns are **mealtime resistance/refusal**, **sensory and texture-related feeding issues**, and **dietary restrictions with highly restricted food preferences** [N2-F2][N3-F3][N3-R5]. These feeding patterns are important because they are linked to **nutrient inadequacy**, **overweight**, and **growth-related effects** [N3-F3][N2-F2][N6-R2]. At the same time, the field faces important limitations: definitions are inconsistent, measurement tools are not fully standardized, and clinical documentation can be subjective or incomplete [N3-F3][N2-F2]. Overall, feeding behavior research is both practical and methodologically complex, with documentation serving as a bridge between behavioral observation and intervention, while also highlighting the need for more consistent and objective measurement in future work [N2-F2][N3-F3][N4-R2][N4-R4].
